title: First week

enter:office@1: Monday, 08:00. The Alder County Medical Examiner's Office. Your first day.
A letter with your name on it is waiting at the front desk.
day:2: Tuesday, 07:55. The light on your desk phone is blinking.
day:3: Wednesday, 09:12. The desk phone is blinking again.
day:4: Thursday, 07:30. A message came in late last night, after you'd gone home.
day:5: Friday. The intake board is quiet for once. Dr. Achterberg has the coffee on.
read:desk-note-day1: You switch off the desk lamp and head home.
read:desk-note-day2: You fold Ray's note into your pocket and head home.
read:desk-note-day3: You take a slice of lemon cake, as instructed, and head home.
read:desk-note-day4: You sit for a moment with the lamp on. Then you switch it off and head home.
case-started:night-shift: That's the one. Van's in the garage when you're ready, Doc.
case-started:kitchen-floor: Juniper Street. Her daughter's waiting at the house. Van's in the garage.
case-started:basement-stairs: Police have held the house since last night. Van's in the garage.
procedure:night-shift:scene: Patrol was first in. They'll tell you what they touched, but ask anyway. Always ask.
procedure:kitchen-floor:scene: The daughter is Ruth. She found her mother this morning. Go gently with her.
procedure:basement-stairs:scene: His wife is in the front room with an officer. You can speak with her when you're ready.
Look at everything once before you decide anything. Same as any scene.
procedure:*:external: Head to toe, region by region. Say what you see, not what you think it means. Meaning comes later.
procedure:*:autopsy: I'll assist. Take your time; nobody hurries in here.
procedure:*:tox: Sample's in. Rush run, so you'll have it within the hour.
procedure:*:xray: Skeletal survey's set up. Every bone, old breaks and new.
enter:scene-night-shift: Cutler Lane. A small, neat house. The bedroom is at the back.
enter:scene-kitchen-floor: Juniper Street. A bright kitchen, a kettle, a calendar full of handwriting.
enter:scene-basement-stairs: Birch Hollow Road. The basement door stands open at the end of the hall.
turn:basement-stairs: Before you go on. What time did Mrs. Ortiz say he fell?
About an hour before she called. She called at 23:05.
Then read me what you've just written down, and ask yourself whether a body does that in an hour.
Work out a window from the body alone. Then set her account beside it. When the two disagree, we don't pick a side; we find out why.
signed:night-shift: You sign. Marcus Hale, 58, a retired bus mechanic who coached his niece's softball team. The certificate is the last official word on his life.
signed:kitchen-floor: You sign. Eleanor Voss, 81, a former school librarian who still walked to the market every morning. The certificate is the last official word on her life.
signed:basement-stairs: You sign. Tomás Ortiz, 45, a high-school chemistry teacher. The certificate is the last official word on his life, and others will rely on it.

day1: You must be our new examiner. Miriam Achterberg. Welcome.
Three rules for the week. Look before you decide. Write what you see in plain words. And never let one clue outvote all the others.
Ray drives the van and runs our scenes; he's in the garage. Priya runs the lab. Go and say hello to both of them.
day1:tour: Ray's in the garage and Priya's in the lab. And read the poster by the exam table. It's older than Priya, and it's still right.
day1:evening: That's enough for a first day. I left you a note on your desk. Then go home.
morning: Today's folder is on the intake board. Take it when you're ready.
case:night-shift: Start where he was found. The room matters as much as the body: what it was like overnight, not just when we arrived.
case:kitchen-floor: Eighty-one, and living on her own. Find out what she took every day, and why. Older bodies keep their histories in the medicine cabinet.
case:basement-stairs: Police are involved because nobody saw what happened. That's routine. Our job is exactly what it was on Tuesday.
case:basement-stairs:flagged: Keep going. The body gives you a window; the account gives you a time. Put both on the certificate's evidence and see where they land.
evening: Go home. There's a note on your desk first.
default: Questions are free in this office. Wrong certificates aren't.

day1: Ray Delgado, death investigator. I drive the van, I talk to families, and I photograph everything twice.
When we go out, the scene is yours to look at, but nothing gets moved until it's photographed.
Logbook's on the dash if you ever want to know where I've been.
morning: Van's warm. Grab the folder off the board and we'll go.
case:night-shift: The neighbor's name is Walt. They looked out for each other, those two.
case:kitchen-floor: Her daughter rings her most nights, she says. Families notice when a routine breaks.
case:basement-stairs: Officers took a statement last night. Ours is separate. We write down what she tells us, word for word.
debrief: Doc Achterberg reads every certificate. Mine too, back when I filled them in.
default: Van's fueled. Kit's stocked. Quiet's good, in this job.

day1: Priya Natarajan, lab and toxicology. You send me blood, I tell you what's in it and how much.
A rush run costs the county real money. Order it when it could change your certificate, which is more often than people think.
case:night-shift: If he was on a prescription, the level tells you whether he took it as directed. Too little, too much, or just right.
case:kitchen-floor: Anything in the medicine cabinet, bring me the name. I'll know what level to look for.
case:basement-stairs: Alcohol's the first thing people ask about with a fall. The number will tell you whether it matters.
default: Centrifuge is humming, so all is well. Need anything run?

case: I'm Walt, from next door. I've got his key; we look out for each other.
We ate dinner together at mine, around ten last night. Thirty years on night shifts at the bus depot, so ten o'clock was dinnertime for him.
He went home at a quarter to eleven. Said he was a little tired. That's all. A little tired.
This morning he didn't answer the door, so I let myself in. That was twenty to eight. He was in bed.
I phoned her at half past eight last night, like most nights. She told me about the market. She sounded well. Completely herself.
This morning she didn't answer the phone. She always answers. So I drove over, and I found her here at nine.
Her medicines are in the cabinet over the sink, if you need them.
default: Thank you for taking care with her.

case: He fell down the stairs. About an hour before I called.
I called at five past eleven.
She looks toward the basement door, then away.
default: Please just tell me what happened to him.

intro: I've read your certificate for {name}. {score} out of {max}.

lines: This is clean. Time, cause and manner, each one tied to evidence. I'd sign it myself.
Good work. A couple of places where your evidence and your boxes don't quite line up. The review on the terminal shows which.
It's a start. Parts of this rest on less than they should. Go back through the review before tomorrow.
We'll go through this one together. That's what the first week is for. Nobody signs a perfect first certificate.

night-shift: The thing I'd want you to take from Mr. Hale is the window. A room that was cold overnight cools a body faster than the 70 °F we measured, so the usual rate would have put his death too early.
He died of heart disease he didn't know was that severe. 'A little tired' after dinner was probably an early warning. That's a natural death, and it was still worth every step.
kitchen-floor: Mrs. Voss is about the warfarin. A fall most people walk away from can be fatal on a blood thinner.
Still an accident. The fall caused the injury; the medicine made the bleed worse, taken exactly as prescribed. One clue doesn't outvote the rest.
basement-stairs: Mr. Ortiz was the one this week was building to. The body said hours; the account said one. When they disagree that much, the body is usually the more reliable witness.

His injuries were on top of the head, with defense bruises on his forearms and no fractures from a tumble. Homicide on a certificate is a medical finding, not a verdict. What happens next is for the police and the courts.

close: Now go and read the note on your desk, and go home.
replay: Another look at an old case. {score} out of {max} this time. Practice is how examiners get good.

endOfWeek: That's your first week. {count} certificates, {total} out of {max} between them.
Marcus Hale, Eleanor Voss, Tomás Ortiz. Each of them got a careful answer. That's the job, and you did it.
The board fills up again on Monday. Until then, any of this week's folders is yours to work again.
